docs.title: ScriptO Studio
docs.text: Tell your board what to do. An agent writes the MicroPython, tries it on your real hardware and leaves it running on the board. You watch every call, and you can stop it at any moment.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Set up a board and connect
  • Make your first ScriptO
  • Use Studio's agent, which runs in the browser with nothing to install
  • Connect Claude Code or another agent

docs.title: The words used here
docs.text: Studio The app you run in a browser or install. It's where you work with an agent and watch what it does. Board An ESP32 running MicroPython and Studio's firmware. Each board is an MCP server, so any agent that speaks MCP can use it. ScriptO MicroPython left on the board to stay. It keeps running with nobody connected and can start at boot. It's what an agent leaves behind. See ScriptOs. App A ScriptO with a browser side as well, for tools that need a screen, like OpenInverter. See Apps. MCP The Model Context Protocol, the open standard that agents use to call tools. It's the board's only protocol, and Studio uses it too.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
The board is the source of truth. What's installed, what runs at boot, what tools exist and what hardware it has all live on the board, so any agent finds them there.

  • Studio's agent runs in the page, on your own OpenRouter key.
  • Outside agents like Claude Code run on your computer and connect to the board directly. They keep your repos, your shell and their own tools.
  • Studio stays connected beside them and shows every call as it happens.

Read how agents work with a board for more, or the architecture for how it's built.

docs.title: How Agents Work with a Board
docs.text:
An agent is a model with tools. A board gives it tools over MCP: run code, read and write files, make ScriptOs. There are three ways to run one, and they all use those same tools.

Studio's agent An outside agent PFC Runs in The browser page Your computer The board Install Nothing The agent, such as Claude Code An App Model Yours on OpenRouter Whatever the agent uses A provider you configure Reaches One board Your repos, shell and other tools as well Its own board Asks first In the chat In its own prompts

Use Studio's agent to get something working on a board. Use an outside agent when the work also needs your repos or a shell.

docs.title: What makes this work
docs.text:
The board explains itself. When an agent connects, the board tells it the rules and its hardware, built from its manifest, so the agent needs no setup. See What a Board Tells an Agent.

The agent can try things. exec runs Python on the board and returns what it printed, so an agent can check a pin or a sensor instead of assuming. It stops after 4 seconds, and longer work belongs in a ScriptO.

The work stays. scripto_create leaves code on the board that keeps running with nobody connected. See ScriptOs.

A person can see it. Studio stays connected beside the agent, and the board reports every agent call to it.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: The agent Where it shows Runs exec Code and output in the terminal, tagged with the client's name Changes something on the board A dim line in the terminal, or a red one if it failed Finishes any call A line in the Logs window, with its name and how long it took Writes or removes a file The file list refreshes, and an open tab reloads unless it has unsaved edits Creates or changes a ScriptO Its row in the sidebar updates

docs.title: What keeps it safe
docs.text:
Connecting takes a password, and an agent gets less than a person does. Its exec stops after 4 seconds where a person's can run for 60, it can only break its own call, and it can't arm CAN transmit.

That protects against accidents. It isn't a sandbox, because exec runs any Python. Don't give an agent a board you wouldn't trust it with, and don't connect a board to anything it could damage without someone watching.

All the tools are listed in the MCP tools reference.

docs.title: Compared with a bridge on your computer
docs.text:
Another way to give an agent a board is an MCP server on your computer that drives MicroPython's REPL, such as mcp-micropython-bridge. Both give the agent general tools, so it writes code rather than picking from a menu. They differ in where MCP runs.

A bridge on your computer ScriptO Studio MCP runs on Your computer, which types into the REPL The board Firmware Standard MicroPython, on any port ScriptO Studio's firmware On your computer Python and the bridge, and a USB cable or the REPL set up on Wi-Fi A browser, or any MCP client Clients at once One, which holds the REPL Several, so a person can watch while an agent works While the agent works The REPL is the agent's, so a program running on the board is stopped first ScriptOs keep running, and exec shares the interpreter with them When code hangs Ctrl-C down the same line The connection is held in C beneath MicroPython, so it stays up and interrupt breaks the call What the agent knows of the hardware A notes file it writes and reads itself The board's manifest, and what you've wired once an agent has it working, given to every client when it connects More tools A fixed set Apps add tools for their hardware

A bridge suits any board running standard MicroPython, worked on from one computer. ScriptO Studio suits a board that keeps running on its own, that you reach from anywhere on your network with nothing installed, and that a person can watch while an agent works.

docs.title: What a Board Tells an Agent
docs.text: When a client connects, the board's MCP instructions tell it how to work and what hardware it has. An agent given nothing else, with no shell, files or notes, can make a working ScriptO from this alone.

docs.title: What's in it
docs.text:
The rules. Use only pins in the hardware list or ones the person says they've wired, because a wrong pin can fight what's on it, and record what they've wired once it works. Try hardware with exec before relying on it, and see what it reads at rest. Say only what you saw, and ask the person to try what only they can see or hear.

The hardware. The board's identity, devices, resources and capabilities, built from its manifest at /settings/board.json, and what's been wired to it, from /settings/wired.json. device_info returns the same facts.

Tool descriptions. A rule about one tool lives in that tool's description, such as how can_capture finds a signal, so every board with that tool gets it.

docs.title: Adding how-to text to a device
docs.text:
A device's description in the manifest is where its how-to goes:

"imu": {
  "type": "LIS3DH",
  "bus": "i2c.i2c0",
  "i2c_address": "0x19",
  "description": "3-axis accelerometer. from lib.sys import imu, then imu.read() gives x, y and z in milli-g, and wakes it the first time."
}

Some things make a difference:

  • Write a helper as its literal import line. "imu.read() from lib.sys.imu" reads like from lib.sys.imu import imu, and agents write that and crash.
  • Say what normal looks like. "At rest, gravity reads about 1000 mg" tells an agent what to compare with.
  • Say when there's no driver. "No MicroPython driver yet" stops an agent trying.
  • Keep the whole thing under about 4 KB. Claude Code cuts server instructions at around 4,096 characters. Devices come before resources and capabilities, so they're the last to go, and device_info always has everything.

See Board Configurations for the rest of the manifest.

docs.title: What you wire
docs.text:
The manifest knows what's on the board, not what you've added to it. Tell the agent once what you've wired and to which pins. When it has it working, it records it with wired_add, and every later session sees it with the board's own hardware:

"door": {
  "type": "switch",
  "pin": 2,
  "description": "Reed switch to GND. from lib.wired.door import door, then door.shut() is True when the door is shut."
}
  • Code uses names. board.pin("door") returns 2, and a device on a bus is board.device("bme280"), so moving a wire means updating the record, not the code.
  • Helpers stay. The agent puts a helper in /lib/wired/ and names it in the description, so the next agent uses it rather than starting again.
  • Pins are checked. wired_add refuses a pin the board already uses, one the chip's flash or PSRAM holds, or one something else is wired to.
  • Default buses give way. On a bare dev board the manifest's I2C, SPI and CAN pins are only where those buses go by default. Wire a switch to one, and that bus is left out while the switch is recorded. A sensor on the default I2C bus names the bus instead, as i2c.i2c0, and shares it.

wired_remove takes something out when you disconnect it. What's wired lives apart from the manifest, so Studio's manifest updates never touch it.

docs.title: Other Agents
docs.text: Every board is an MCP server, so any MCP client can use it. An agent on your computer keeps your repos, your shell and its own tools, and Studio shows what it does on the board.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
1. Connect Studio to the board.
  2. Open System > Agent.
  3. Copy the line under Claude Code and paste it into a terminal, once, from any folder.
  4. Start a new Claude Code session and ask it something, like "plot a sine wave on the board's terminal".

The line looks like this:

claude mcp add --scope user --transport http <board> http://<board>/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer <agent token>"

The token is hidden on screen and included in what you copy. It lets whoever has it run code on the board, so treat it like a password.

docs.title: Any other client
docs.text:
Other agents, in the same panel, gives the address and the header to use with any MCP client that speaks HTTP.

A client that keeps a WebSocket open at wss://<board>/mcp gets more: live progress from long tools, and it can break its own blocked exec. See the MCP tools reference.

docs.title: Watching it work
docs.text:
Stay connected in Studio. The agent's calls appear under Other agents on Home, and its code and output appear in the terminal, tagged with its name.

Stop under Other agents breaks whatever it's running, and stops ScriptOs and Apps too.

Permission prompts belong to the agent you're using, so Studio doesn't ask on its behalf.

docs.title: ss-relay
docs.text:
ss-relay is a small stdio MCP server you can run beside an agent. It passes the board's tools through and adds what needs your computer: syncing a folder by hash, moving files by path, discovery and flashing. It also suits a client that only speaks stdio.

claude mcp add pybot -e SS_RELAY_PASSWORD=<password> -- uvx ss-relay --device wss://pybot-6014.local/mcp

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Plain HTTP isn't encrypted. The default line uses it because agents won't accept a board's self-signed certificate, so the token crosses your network in clear. Use it on a network you trust.
  • A board holds three WebSockets. A fourth client is refused with a message saying why, and nobody is pushed off. Studio holds one, and a second once its own agent has run. A client on plain HTTP holds none.
  • A ScriptO's long tools work differently over HTTP. They return a job id to poll with job_status, and can't report live progress.
  • Tool lists can change. Installing a ScriptO or App can add tools. A long-running session may keep the list it started with, so start a new one if a tool seems to be missing.

docs.title: An agent with no computer
docs.text: PFC is an App that runs an agent on the board itself. Install it from Apps.

docs.title: Studio's Agent
docs.text: Studio's agent runs in the browser page on Home. There's nothing to install. It works on one board, with that board's tools, and it's meant for getting something working on the board rather than for general coding.

docs.title: Your key and model
docs.text:
Studio's agent uses models through OpenRouter, billed to your account.

  • API key under the message box adds or changes your key. It stays in this browser, in a separate frame that Studio's pages and Apps can't read. Studio can ask that frame for a reply, but it can't read the key or choose where it's sent.
  • The model's name beside it opens the model list, which you can search. Tick Free only to see the free ones. Any model that supports tools will do.

Free models have daily limits and vary in how well they use tools. If one struggles, try another.

docs.title: Asking
docs.text:
Type a request and press Enter, or Shift+Enter for a new line. If a ScriptO crashes, Ask agent on its row attaches the error to your next message.

The chat shows each of the agent's calls, and hovering over one shows its full output. What it runs with exec also appears in the terminal.

docs.title: When it asks first
docs.text:
The agent asks before what's hard to undo:

  • Deleting a file
  • Writing a file outside a ScriptO's own folder
  • Replacing or removing a ScriptO it didn't make in this chat
  • Resetting the board, or stopping user tasks
  • exec code that plainly erases, flashes or resets
  • A destructive tool added by a ScriptO or App

Choose Allow, Allow for this chat or Deny. If you deny it, the agent is told, and carries on without it or asks you.

This guards against accidents and isn't a sandbox. exec runs any Python, and the scan only catches what's plain to see.

docs.title: Stopping it
docs.text: Stop beside the message box ends the agent and its current call, and leaves the board's ScriptOs running. Stop above the editor goes further, and stops ScriptOs and Apps too.

docs.title: Long chats
docs.text:
A chat stays when you reload the page, one for each board, until you click New chat. If the page closed partway through a request, the chat says it stopped there, and the agent is told which calls may have run. "Allow for this chat" doesn't carry over a reload, so it asks again.

The chat is stored in your browser, and it includes whatever the board printed.

To keep costs and limits in check:

  • The model gets at most 20,000 characters of any one tool's output, keeping the start and the end. You can still see all of it by hovering over the call.
  • When a chat gets long, its history is replaced by a summary written by the same model, plus your latest request word for word. A note in the chat says so, and hovering over the note shows the summary. Everything stays on your screen.
  • A request stops after 40 rounds of tool calls. Tell it to carry on if it should.

docs.title: Selecting text
docs.text: Click in the chat and press Cmd-A or Ctrl-A to select all of it, in order, ready to copy.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text: An App is a ScriptO with a browser side. The board half is MicroPython in /lib/ext/<folder>/, like any ScriptO. The browser half is JavaScript that adds panels to Studio's menu, under Apps, so you can configure the board and watch what it's doing.

docs.title: Apps and ScriptOs
docs.text:
ScriptO App Written in MicroPython MicroPython on the board, JavaScript in Studio Made by An agent, with scripto_create A developer, published to ScriptoHub Where you see it In the sidebar's list of ScriptOs As panels under Apps in the menu Installed from Nothing to install: it's on the board ScriptoHub, from Studio

Both live on the board. The panels only exist while Studio is open. If the App has a main.py or tools for agents, those keep working with no browser connected.

docs.title: Installing an App
docs.text:
Click the + beside Apps in the menu. The library lists what's available and what's installed, with Update and Uninstall for installed ones. You can also click Browse apps on Home to look through ScriptoHub at scriptohub.ai/extensions.

Studio keeps the downloaded bundle in your browser's IndexedDB. When the App has an onInstall hook, Studio runs it with the board connected, and the hook writes the App's device files. The board records the install in /lib/ext/registry.json, so any browser or agent connecting later sees the same list.

If you install while no board is connected, Studio saves the bundle and finishes the device install when you connect and open the App.

Uninstalling removes the App's code from the board. Its data stays.

docs.title: What an App can add
docs.text:
• Panels in the menu, drawn by a JavaScript class.
  • MicroPython libraries, in /lib/ext/<folder>/.
  • A main.py with async def run() that runs on the board, and can start at every boot.
  • Tools for agents, as files in tools/. They appear as <app>_<tool>.

docs.title: App API
docs.text: What the browser side of an App can use.

docs.title: Constructor arguments
docs.text:
Your App's class receives four arguments:

constructor(deviceAPI, emit, state, html) {
  this.device = deviceAPI  // Device communication
  this.emit = emit         // Event emitter
  this.state = state       // Shared state
  this.html = html         // Template renderer
}

docs.title: Device API
docs.text: The deviceAPI object provides device communication:

docs.title: execute(code)
docs.text:
Execute Python code on the device. Returns output as a string.

const result = await this.device.execute('print(1 + 1)')
// result = "2"

docs.title: saveFile(path, content)
docs.text:
Write a file to the device filesystem.

await this.device.saveFile('/lib/my_module.py', 'print("hello")')

docs.title: mkdir(path)
docs.text:
Create a directory. Succeeds silently if directory exists.

await this.device.mkdir('/lib/ext/my_app')

docs.title: subscribe(type, handler) and unsubscribe(type)
docs.text:
Listen for an event the board sends. type is a key in the event, and handler gets that key's value. There is one handler per type, so subscribing again replaces it.

this.device.subscribe('my_event', (value) => {
  this.state.myApp.last = value
  this.emit('render')
})
// later
this.device.unsubscribe('my_event')

docs.title: openCanStream({ ack, onFrames })
docs.text:
Receive every frame the CAN bus gets. onFrames(payload, lost) is called with whole 20-byte records, laid out as lib/sys/streams.py on the board says, and with how many frames were lost just before them. It returns a promise of { status(), close() }.

const stream = await this.device.openCanStream({
  onFrames: (payload, lost) => this.handleFrames(payload, lost)
})
// later
await stream.close()

docs.title: State Object
docs.text:
The state object is shared by all Apps and Studio:

// Read connection status
if (this.state.isConnected) {
  // Device is connected
}

// Store your App's data
if (!this.state.myApp) {
  this.state.myApp = { config: {} }
}

docs.title: State properties
docs.text: Property Type Description isConnected boolean A board is connected

docs.title: Emit Function
docs.text:
Trigger events in the application:

// Re-render the current panel
this.emit('render')

// Refresh the file listing
this.emit('refresh-files')

docs.title: HTML Template
docs.text:
The html function is a tagged template literal for rendering:

renderMyPanel() {
  const items = ['A', 'B', 'C']

  return this.html`
    <div class="system-panel">
      <div class="panel-header">
        <h2>My Panel</h2>
      </div>
      <ul>
        ${items.map(item => this.html`<li>${item}</li>`)}
      </ul>
    </div>
  `
}

docs.title: Event Handlers
docs.text:
Use onclick, onchange, etc. with arrow functions:

return this.html`
  <button onclick=${() => this.handleClick()}>
    Click Me
  </button>
  <input 
    type="text" 
    value=${this.state.myApp.name}
    oninput=${(e) => this.handleInput(e.target.value)}
  />
`

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
return this.html`
  ${this.state.isConnected
    ? this.html`<p>Connected!</p>`
    : this.html`<p>Not connected</p>`
  }
`

docs.title: onInstall()
docs.text:
Called when the user installs the App with a board connected:

async onInstall() {
  // this.deviceFiles is injected by the loader
  for (const [path, content] of Object.entries(this.deviceFiles)) {
    await this.device.saveFile(path, content)
  }
  return true  // Return false to indicate failure
}

docs.title: getMenuItems()
docs.text:
Optional. Return dynamic menu items:

getMenuItems() {
  const items = [{ id: 'main', label: 'Main' }]

  // Add items based on state
  if (this.state.devices?.length > 0) {
    this.state.devices.forEach(d => {
      items.push({ id: `device-${d.id}`, label: d.name })
    })
  }

  return items
}

docs.title: CSS Classes
docs.text:
Use these system classes for consistent styling:

Class Description .system-panel Standard panel container .panel-header Panel header with h2 and actions .panel-message Centered message text

Define your App's styles in extension.json:

{
  "styles": ".my-btn { background: var(--scheme-primary); }"
}

docs.title: Device Libraries
docs.text: An App can bundle MicroPython files that go on the board when it's installed.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Device files live in the device/ directory of your App:

MyApp/
├── extension.json
├── src/
│   └── index.js
└── device/
    └── helpers.py

docs.title: devicePaths Mapping
docs.text:
In extension.json, map files under device/ to where they go on the board:

{
  "devicePaths": {
    "helpers.py": "/lib/ext/my_app/helpers.py",
    "utils.py": "/lib/ext/my_app/utils.py",
    "submodule/__init__.py": "/lib/ext/my_app/submodule/__init__.py"
  }
}

Device files go to /lib/ext/<folder>/. Use underscores in the folder name, since a hyphen can't appear in a Python module name.

docs.title: Installation Flow
docs.text:
1. You click Install in the App library.
  2. Studio downloads the bundle and stores it in the browser.
  3. With a board connected, Studio calls onInstall() on the App.
  4. The App writes the files in this.deviceFiles to the board.
  5. Studio records the install on the board in /lib/ext/registry.json.

An agent or script that copies the files itself can record the install with the scripto_installed tool. It takes id, version, and optionally name and folder (the folder under /lib/ext/, when it differs from the id with hyphens turned into underscores). Call it once the files are in place.

docs.title: onInstall Implementation
docs.text:
async onInstall() {
  if (!this.state.isConnected) return false

  try {
    // Create directories
    await this.device.mkdir('/lib/ext/my_app')
    await this.device.mkdir('/lib/ext/my_app/submodule')

    // Write all device files
    for (const [path, content] of Object.entries(this.deviceFiles)) {
      console.log(`Writing ${path}...`)
      await this.device.saveFile(path, content)
    }

    return true
  } catch (e) {
    console.error('Installation failed:', e)
    return false
  }
}

docs.title: Import Paths
docs.text:
Device code imports from the installed path:

from lib.ext.my_app.helpers import my_function

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Keep files small - Device flash is limited
  2. Avoid heavy dependencies - Files should be self-contained
  3. Use lazy imports - Import modules only when needed
  4. Don't verify imports in onInstall - an import can fail if a file it needs isn't written yet

docs.title: Bundle Process
docs.text:
The bundler: 1. Reads devicePaths from extension.json 2. Reads each source file from device/ 3. Base64-encodes the content 4. Embeds as __DEVICE_FILES__ in the bundle

At runtime, the loader decodes __DEVICE_FILES__ and injects it as instance.deviceFiles.

docs.title: App versioning
docs.text: Bump the version in an App's extension.json whenever you change it. ScriptoHub and Studio use it to decide whether an update is available.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
A version is an array of three numbers, [major, minor, patch]:

"version": [1, 2, 0]

docs.title: Before you publish
docs.text:
• [ ] Bump version in extension.json.
  • [ ] Test the App with the change.
  • [ ] Commit the code and the version bump together.

Use a patch bump for a fix and a minor bump for a feature.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• The App library shows Update available when ScriptoHub has a newer version than the one installed.
  • The board records the installed version in /lib/ext/registry.json.
  • Without a bump, browsers keep running the code they've already stored.

docs.title: Writing Apps
docs.text: An App is a JavaScript class that provides panels in Studio, plus the MicroPython files that go on the board. See Apps for what that means for users.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
An App's source is bundled into one file for distribution:

MyApp/
├── extension.json          # Metadata and configuration
├── src/
│   └── index.js           # Entry point (exports class)
└── device/                 # Files that go on the board (optional)
    ├── my_helpers.py
    ├── main.py            # Runs on the board (optional)
    └── tools/
        └── read_status.py # A tool for agents (optional)

docs.title: extension.json
docs.text:
The manifest defines your App:

{
  "name": "My App",
  "id": "my-app",
  "version": [1, 0, 0],
  "author": "Your Name",
  "description": "What your App does",
  "icon": "settings",
  "menu": [
    { "id": "config", "label": "Configuration" },
    { "id": "status", "label": "Status" }
  ],
  "styles": ".my-class { color: blue; }",
  "devicePaths": {
    "my_helpers.py": "/lib/ext/my_app/my_helpers.py"
  }
}

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Required Description name ✓ Display name id ✓ Unique identifier (lowercase, hyphens) version ✓ Semver array [major, minor, patch] author ✓ Your name or organization description ✓ Brief description icon Tabler icon name (e.g., bolt, battery-charging) iconSvg Custom SVG icon (overrides icon) menu Array of menu items with id and label styles CSS injected when the App loads devicePaths Map of source → device paths for bundler

docs.title: The class
docs.text:
Create src/index.js with a class that is the default export:

class MyApp {
  constructor(deviceAPI, emit, state, html) {
    this.device = deviceAPI  // Device communication
    this.emit = emit         // Trigger re-render
    this.state = state       // Shared state object
    this.html = html         // Tagged template literal for rendering

    // Initialize your App's state
    if (!this.state.myApp) {
      this.state.myApp = {
        config: {},
        status: 'idle'
      }
    }
  }

  // Render each menu tab
  renderConfig() {
    return this.html`
      <div class="system-panel">
        <div class="panel-header">
          <h2>Configuration</h2>
        </div>
        <div style="padding: 20px;">
          <p>Your configuration UI here</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    `
  }

  renderStatus() {
    return this.html`
      <div class="system-panel">
        <div class="panel-header">
          <h2>Status</h2>
        </div>
        <div style="padding: 20px;">
          <p>Status: ${this.state.myApp.status}</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    `
  }
}

export { MyApp as default }

docs.title: Render Methods
docs.text: For each menu item with id: "foo", implement renderFoo() (capitalized). The method should return a template literal using this.html.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text:
• Use this.state for persistent data shared across renders
  • Call this.emit('render') to trigger a re-render after state changes
  • State persists across panel switches

docs.title: Device Files
docs.text: Device-side Python files live in device/ and get deployed during installation.

docs.title: devicePaths mapping
docs.text:
In extension.json, map source files under device/ to board paths:

{
  "devicePaths": {
    "helpers.py": "/lib/ext/my_app/helpers.py",
    "main.py": "/lib/ext/my_app/main.py",
    "tools/read_status.py": "/lib/ext/my_app/tools/read_status.py"
  }
}

Device files go to /lib/ext/<folder>/. Use underscores in the folder name, because Python can't import a name with a hyphen. Without devicePaths, the bundler puts everything under device/ in /lib/ext/<id>/.

docs.title: main.py
docs.text: /lib/ext/<folder>/main.py with an async def run() works as it does for a ScriptO. It loops and awaits often, because one interpreter runs everything. It can start at every boot.

docs.title: tools/
docs.text:
Each file in /lib/ext/<folder>/tools/ becomes a tool that agents can call, named <app>_<file>. Files starting with _ aren't tools. A tool has a configuration block that gives its name, description and arguments, and an async def run(args, job):

# === START_CONFIG_PARAMETERS ===
dict(
    info = dict(
        name = "Read status",
        description = "What an agent reads to decide to use this.",
        effects = dict(readOnly=True, destructive=False, openWorld=False),
    ),
    args = dict(
        name = dict(label="Parameter name", type=str),
    ),
)
# === END_CONFIG_PARAMETERS ===

async def run(args, job):
    job.progress(1, 2, "halfway")
    return {"value": 1}

Effects you leave out take the conservative defaults.

docs.title: onInstall hook
docs.text:
Implement onInstall() to write the device files:

async onInstall() {
  if (!this.state.isConnected) return false

  try {
    // Create directories
    await this.device.mkdir('/lib/ext/my_app')

    // Write all device files (injected by loader)
    for (const [path, content] of Object.entries(this.deviceFiles)) {
      await this.device.saveFile(path, content)
    }

    return true
  } catch (e) {
    console.error('Installation failed:', e)
    return false
  }
}

The this.deviceFiles object is injected by the loader and contains base64-decoded file contents keyed by target path.

docs.title: Device API
docs.text:
Use this.device to talk to the connected board. The full list is in the App API.

Method Description device.execute(code) Run Python code, returns output device.saveFile(path, content) Write file to device device.mkdir(path) Create directory 
// Example: Get config from device
async getConfig() {
  const result = await this.device.execute(`
    from lib.ext.my_app.helpers import get_config
    import json
    print(json.dumps(get_config()))
  `)
  return JSON.parse(result)
}

docs.title: Bundling
docs.text:
tools/bundle_extensions.js in the PFC repository builds a bundle. It needs esbuild (npm install in that repository):

# Writes each bundle into its App's directory
node tools/bundle_extensions.js --extensions-dir /path/to/your/apps

# Or collect the bundles in one place
node tools/bundle_extensions.js \
  --extensions-dir /path/to/your/apps \
  --output-dir /path/to/bundles

Add --mpy to cross-compile the .py files to .mpy (it needs mpy-cross).

The bundler: 1. Reads extension.json for metadata 2. Bundles JS from src/index.js using esbuild 3. Base64-encodes device files from device/ 4. Produces a single {id}.bundle.js file

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The board is the server, and everything else is a client of it. Studio, Studio's agent and outside agents all use the same dispatcher and the same tools.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text: Repository Holds pyDirect Firmware: C modules on MicroPython v1.29 and ESP-IDF 5.5.1 botiq botIQ: the device scripts (lib/sys), the board manifests, their tests, ss-relay, and the workflow that signs and publishes platform releases scriptostudio This site and the built app scripto-studio Studio, the browser app PFC The agent that runs on the board scriptohub The App catalogue, and every release a board installs: firmware builds, platform releases with their board manifests, and product releases

docs.title: The board
docs.text:
Every message lands in one dispatcher, lib/sys/mcp.py, whichever carrier brought it. See the MCP tools reference for the tools, carriers and tokens.

All Python runs on one interpreter thread, and that shapes the rest. A blocking call holds up every client and ScriptO, so anything that must work while Python is blocked is in C (mcplink, wsserver, httpserver): token checks, breaking a call, the output rings and CAN capture. Tools, ScriptOs and policy are Python, so they update without a reflash.

events.py tells sockets holding a human token about every agent call and file write, and that's how Studio shows what an agent is doing. Its Stop button sends a control frame that C acts on at once.

docs.title: Studio
docs.text: Studio is a browser app with no server of its own, written in strict ES modules on choo and nanohtml and built with Vite. It holds its own socket to the board with the human token.

docs.title: Studio's agent
docs.text:
The agent is a tool loop in the page. It lists the board's tools, sends them to the model with the board's own instructions, runs each call on its own socket with the agent token, and repeats until the model stops calling tools.

The key is kept apart. Model calls go through an iframe on another origin, which holds the OpenRouter key, because Apps run in Studio's page and could read anything stored there. Studio can ask that frame for a reply, but can't read the key or choose where it's sent.

Everything is an event. Each request, reply, call, result, answer and note is appended to a log in IndexedDB, with one chat per board. One function applies an event both as it happens and when a reload replays it. A tab holds a Web Lock on a board's log, so two tabs can't interleave their events.

History only grows. On recent Claude models, each block of reasoning is bound to the system prompt, the tools and every message before it, so changing any of them makes later reasoning invalid. So:

  • Tool output is cut once, as it arrives, and never edited afterwards.
  • A long chat is replaced whole by a summary and the latest request, with no tail of tool calls kept.
  • All reasoning is dropped when the model, system prompt or tool list changes, and after a reload. Dropping all of it is valid, and dropping some from the middle isn't.

If the API still says the chat is too long or its reasoning is stale, the agent recovers and retries once.

docs.title: ScriptOs
docs.text: /lib/ext/registry.json is the record of what's installed, and it's on the board so that any client gets the same answer. See ScriptOs. Every way a ScriptO ends is recorded and shown on its row.

docs.title: Limits to design around
docs.text:
• A board holds three WebSockets, and nothing is evicted.
  • Plain HTTP has no encryption or live progress.
  • A board is reached on its own network. There's no remote path from Studio.
  • An agent's exec stops after 4 seconds.
  • Studio's crash check only sees the first two seconds after a ScriptO starts. Later failures show on its row.

docs.title: Display drivers
docs.text: The board manifest names a display, and lib/sys/display/display_manager.py picks the driver from it.

docs.title: Supported displays
docs.text:
Interface Driver Display Resolution IC QSPI spd2010.py Round LCD 412×412 SPD2010 QSPI co5300.py AMOLED 466×466 and 280×456, by board CO5300 SPI st77xx.py Rectangular LCD 240×320, and other sizes by board ST7789 EPD epd_3in97.py, epd_3in97_lvgl.py 3.97" e-paper 800×480 SSD1677

The manifest's devices.display.interface chooses the path: qspi, spi or epd. For QSPI, the driver field chooses between spd2010 (the default) and co5300.

docs.title: Boot Sequence
docs.text:
boot.py calls init_display() on boards with a QSPI or SPI display. On a board with an e-paper display, boot.py calls lib.calmos.init() instead, and that calls init_display(). For a QSPI or SPI display, init_display():

  1. Reads the manifest with board.device("display") to get the interface.
  2. Resets the panel through the I2C GPIO expander, if it's wired that way (QSPI).
  3. Creates the QSPI or SPI bus with the manifest's pins.
  4. Runs the driver's register init sequence.
  5. Clears the screen to black before turning the display on, to avoid a flash.
  6. Draws the 128×128 boot logo from splash.bin in the centre.
  7. Turns the display on and sets the brightness.

For e-paper, init_display() powers the panel through the AXP2101, creates the SPI bus, and initializes the EPD and its LVGL backend.

from lib.sys.display.display_manager import init_display
lcd = init_display(brightness=80)

init_display() returns the existing instance if it has already run. get_display() returns it later, or None before init.

docs.title: QSPI Command Encoding
docs.text:
The SPD2010 and CO5300 use a 32-bit QSPI command format. Due to ESP-IDF's byte reversal in the SPI peripheral, commands must be pre-encoded:

# On wire: PREFIX, 0x00, CMD, 0x00
# Encoding: (cmd << 8) | (prefix << 24)
def _qspi_cmd(cmd):
    return (cmd << 8) | (0x02 << 24)    # 0x02 = write command

def _qspi_color_cmd(cmd):
    return (cmd << 8) | (0x32 << 24)    # 0x32 = write color data

docs.title: DMA and Buffer Sizing
docs.text:
For QSPI displays with PSRAM-backed LVGL draw buffers:

  • Bounce buffer: pre-allocated in internal SRAM by the qspi_lcd C module (BOUNCE_BUF_SIZE). It sets the largest single DMA transfer.
  • Draw buffer factor: factor=32 splits the screen into chunks that fit in the bounce buffer. On a 412×412 panel a chunk is 412 × (412/32) × 2, about 11 KB.
  • Double buffering: off, to save PSRAM.

docs.title: Custom Fonts (TinyTTF)
docs.text:
The build enables TinyTTF for runtime .ttf font loading:

import lvgl as lv
import fs_driver

# Register MicroPython FS bridge (once)
fs_drv = lv.fs_drv_t()
fs_driver.fs_register(fs_drv, 'S')

# Load any TTF at any size
font = lv.tiny_ttf_create_file('S:/lib/fonts/MyFont.ttf', 48)
label.set_style_text_font(font, 0)

Built-in Montserrat sizes: 14, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 48.

docs.title: Using from Scripts
docs.text:
LVGL scripts should not reinitialize the display. Use the boot-initialized driver and just create widgets:

import lvgl as lv

scr = lv.obj()
scr.set_style_bg_color(lv.color_hex(0x000000), 0)

label = lv.label(scr)
label.set_text("Hello World")
label.set_style_text_color(lv.color_hex(0xFFFFFF), 0)
label.set_style_text_font(lv.font_montserrat_36, 0)
label.align(lv.ALIGN.CENTER, 0, 0)

lv.screen_load(scr)

docs.title: MicroPython Quick Reference for ScriptO Studio
docs.text: This document provides a quick reference for MicroPython differences from CPython that are relevant to ScriptO Studio development.

docs.title: Official Documentation
docs.text:
Full MicroPython differences documentation: https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/genrst/

This is the authoritative source for all MicroPython vs CPython differences. Always refer to this when in doubt.

docs.title: Common Gotchas Encountered in This Project
Filesystem Operations
docs.text:
❌ MicroPython does NOT have os.path module

# ❌ WRONG - This will fail
import os.path
path = os.path.join('/lib', 'vehicles', 'zombie_vcu')
dirname = os.path.dirname(__file__)
exists = os.path.exists(path)

# ✅ CORRECT - Use direct string manipulation
path = '/lib/vehicles/zombie_vcu'
# Check existence by trying to open/list
try:
    os.listdir(path)  # If this works, it exists
except OSError:
    pass  # Doesn't exist

Alternatives: - Use string concatenation: f'{base}/{subdir}/{file}' or base + '/' + subdir + '/' + file - Check existence by trying operations: os.listdir(), open(), etc. - Use os.stat() to check if path exists (raises OSError if not)

docs.title: String Methods
docs.text:
❌ MicroPython strings do NOT have .title() method

# ❌ WRONG - This will fail
name = "zombie_vcu".replace('_', ' ').title()  # AttributeError!

# ✅ CORRECT - Implement manually
def title_case(text):
    parts = text.replace('_', ' ').split(' ')
    title_parts = []
    for p in parts:
        if len(p) > 0:
            title_parts.append(p[0].upper() + p[1:])
        else:
            title_parts.append(p)
    return ' '.join(title_parts)

name = title_case("zombie_vcu")  # "Zombie Vcu"

Other string methods that may be missing: - .capitalize() - Implement manually - .title() - Implement manually (as shown above) - .casefold() - May not be available

docs.title: F-Strings
docs.text:
✅ MicroPython DOES support f-strings (Python 3.6+ feature)

# ✅ This works fine
name = "zombie_vcu"
path = f'/lib/vehicles/{name}/{name}.py'

F-strings are supported in MicroPython, so use them freely.

docs.title: Standard Library Modules
docs.text:
Limited standard library - Many CPython modules are not available:

  • ❌ os.path - Not available
  • ❌ pathlib - Not available
  • ❌ importlib.util - Not available
  • ✅ os - Available (but limited - no os.path)
  • ✅ sys - Available
  • ✅ json - Available
  • ✅ time - Available
  • ✅ gc - Available (garbage collector)

Check availability before using: 

try:
    import some_module
except ImportError:
    # Module not available, use alternative
    pass

docs.title: Import System
docs.text:
Package imports work differently:

# ✅ CORRECT - Direct file execution (most reliable)
with open('/lib/vehicles/zombie_vcu/zombie_vcu.py', 'r') as f:
    code = f.read()
exec(code, namespace)

# ⚠️ Package imports may not work if __init__.py is missing
# from vehicles.zombie_vcu import zombie_vcu  # May fail

docs.title: Exception Handling
docs.text:
Exception objects may behave differently:

# ✅ CORRECT - Use str() for string conversion
try:
    # something
except Exception as e:
    error_msg = str(e)  # Works
    # e.message may not exist

docs.title: Dictionary Comprehensions
docs.text:
✅ Dictionary comprehensions work:

# ✅ This works fine
vehicle_list = {k: v['name'] for k, v in VEHICLES.items()}

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text:
File operations work similarly:

# ✅ Standard file operations work
with open('/lib/config.json', 'r') as f:
    data = f.read()

with open('/lib/output.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('content')

docs.title: Memory Constraints
docs.text:
Be mindful of memory:

  • Avoid loading large files into memory at once
  • Use generators where possible
  • Be careful with large lists/dicts
  • Use gc.collect() if needed to force garbage collection

docs.title: Best Practices for ScriptO Studio
docs.text:
1. Always test on actual MicroPython device - Don't assume CPython compatibility
  2. Use try/except for filesystem operations - Check existence by trying operations
  3. Avoid os.path - Use string manipulation instead
  4. Implement missing string methods manually - Don't rely on .title(), .capitalize(), etc.
  5. Keep dependencies minimal - Only use MicroPython standard library
  6. Test imports - Wrap imports in try/except for optional modules
  7. Use f-strings - They're supported and cleaner than .format()

docs.title: Testing Checklist
docs.text:
Before committing code, verify:

  • [ ] No os.path usage
  • [ ] No .title() or .capitalize() on strings
  • [ ] File operations wrapped in try/except
  • [ ] Imports checked for availability
  • [ ] Code tested on actual MicroPython device
  • [ ] Memory usage is reasonable

docs.title: ESP32 port specifics
docs.text:
• MicroPython v1.29 on ESP-IDF 5.5.1
  • Has hardware-specific modules (machine, network, etc.)
  • Every image has ulab: from ulab import numpy as np gives numpy-style arrays and np.fft, and from ulab import scipy gives scipy.signal.sosfilt for filtering.

docs.title: How ScriptO Studio uses the board
docs.text:
• ScriptOs and Apps run as MicroPython on the board.
  • Agents and Studio reach the board through MCP tools over /mcp. See the MCP tools reference.
  • lib.sys.events.notify({"key": value}) sends an event to every connected client. An App's browser side hears it with subscribe.
  • The exec tool runs code in __main__ and returns what it prints.

docs.title: Board Configurations
docs.text:
A board configuration (or "board manifest") is a JSON file that describes the hardware of a specific ESP32 board: its display, pin assignments, buses, sensors, and capabilities. The firmware uses this to set up peripherals without hardcoded board-specific code, so the same firmware binary can drive many different boards.

Studio downloads the manifest for the board you pick during setup and writes it to /settings/board.json on the device. Whenever it connects, it replaces that copy if the published manifest has a later identity.revision. Python code reads it via lib.sys.board:

from lib.sys import board

if board.has("display"):
    disp = board.device("display")
    print(disp.width, disp.height, disp.interface)

led_pin = board.pin("status_led")
uart_cfg = board.uart("primary")

docs.title: When do I need a custom configuration?
docs.text:
Use an existing board config when:

  • Your board is in the list under System > Firmware. Pick it.

Create a custom config when:

  • You have a board that isn't listed (custom PCB, an unsupported dev board, a variant with different wiring).
  • You need to override pin assignments, bus frequencies, or device drivers for an existing board.

docs.title: Where configs live
docs.text:
All board manifests are JSON files in the botiq repository at:

manifests/
├── index.json                          # master list (required)
├── generic_esp32s3.json
├── waveshare_s3_lcd_1.47.json
├── waveshare_s3_amoled_1in75.json
└── ...

index.json names the boards Studio offers in its board dropdown. A manifest left out of it is still published with each release, and Studio doesn't list it.

docs.title: Adding a custom board, step by step
docs.text: We'll walk through adding a fictional "Acme ESP32-S3 Widget Board" with an ST7789 SPI display and a NeoPixel status LED.

docs.title: 1. Create the manifest file
docs.text:
Create manifests/acme_widget_s3.json. The easiest approach is to copy the closest existing board as a starting point. The Waveshare ESP32-S3 LCD 1.47 (waveshare_s3_lcd_1.47.json) is a good template for an S3 + ST7789 SPI LCD board:

{
  "identity": {
    "id": "acme_widget_s3",
    "name": "Acme ESP32-S3 Widget",
    "vendor": "acme",
    "chip": "ESP32-S3",
    "revision": "1.0.0",
    "description": "Acme Widget dev board with 1.3\" ST7789 SPI LCD and NeoPixel"
  },

  "network": {
    "mdns_enabled": true,
    "ap_password": null,
    "default_services": ["http", "mcp"]
  },

  "capabilities": {
    "wifi": true,
    "bluetooth": true,
    "neopixel": true,
    "status_led": true,
    "usb_otg": false,
    "display": true,
    "touch": false,
    "sdcard": false
  },

  "resources": {
    "pins": {
      "status_led": 48,
      "boot": 0
    },

    "spi": {
      "lcd": {
        "sck": 12,
        "mosi": 11,
        "dc": 4,
        "cs": 10,
        "rst": 9
      }
    },

    "uart": {
      "primary": { "tx": 43, "rx": 44 }
    },

    "gpio": {
      "bl_pwm": 5
    }
  },

  "devices": {
    "display": {
      "type": "ST7789",
      "driver": "st7789",
      "bus": "spi.lcd",
      "interface": "spi",
      "width": 240,
      "height": 240,
      "offset_x": 0,
      "offset_y": 0,
      "color_bits": 16,
      "backlight": {
        "pin": 5,
        "active_high": true,
        "pwm_capable": true
      },
      "description": "1.3\" 240x240 IPS LCD"
    },

    "status_led": {
      "type": "neopixel",
      "pin": 48,
      "pixel_order": "GRB",
      "description": "Onboard NeoPixel on GPIO48"
    }
  },

  "memory": {
    "flash_size": "8MB",
    "psram_size": "2MB",
    "psram_mode": "quad"
  }
}

docs.title: 2. Register it in index.json
docs.text:
Add a short entry to manifests/index.json:

{
  "id": "acme_widget_s3",
  "name": "Acme ESP32-S3 Widget",
  "chip": "ESP32-S3",
  "vendor": "acme",
  "description": "Acme Widget dev board with 1.3\" ST7789 SPI LCD and NeoPixel"
}

The id must match the filename (without .json) and the identity.id in the manifest itself.

docs.title: 3. Deploy the manifest
docs.text: Board manifests are published with each platform release on ScriptoHub, and Studio lists the ones in the release it installs. To add a board to the public list, submit a pull request against jetpax/botiq. It appears with the next release.

docs.title: 4. Pick it under System > Firmware
docs.text: After the next release, the board appears in the Board Configuration dropdown on the firmware panel when a matching chip is connected. Selecting it causes Studio to write the manifest to /settings/board.json on the device during provisioning.

docs.title: Top-level sections
docs.text: Section Required Purpose identity yes Board name, vendor, chip family network no mDNS and AP defaults capabilities yes Feature flags (display, wifi, touch, etc.) resources yes Pin assignments and bus configurations devices yes Connected peripherals and their drivers memory no Flash/PSRAM descriptors (informational)

docs.title: identity
docs.text:
"identity": {
  "id": "acme_widget_s3",     // must match filename and index.json id
  "name": "Acme Widget",      // shown in the dropdown
  "vendor": "acme",
  "chip": "ESP32-S3",         // ESP32, ESP32-S3, ESP32-P4
  "revision": "1.0.0",
  "description": "One-line summary shown under the dropdown"
}

Raise revision whenever you change a published manifest. Studio compares it with the copy on each board it connects to and replaces an older copy, so boards set up earlier get the change, along with any edits made to that copy.

docs.title: capabilities
docs.text:
Boolean flags queried by firmware code via board.has("name"). Common keys:

Key Meaning wifi Has WiFi hardware bluetooth Has Bluetooth hardware ethernet Has wired Ethernet PHY usb_otg Has USB-OTG capable port display Has an attached display (see devices.display) touch Has touch input sdcard Has SD card slot neopixel Has one or more WS2812-style LEDs status_led Has a dedicated status LED (may be neopixel) battery Has battery input / fuel gauge imu Has accelerometer/gyro rtc Has battery-backed real-time clock audio Has audio I/O (codec, speaker, mic) gnss Has GNSS/GPS receiver gpio_expander Uses an I/O expander for board pins

You can add custom flags, and anything board.has() queries will work as long as the key exists in this dict.

docs.title: resources.pins
docs.text:
Direct GPIO assignments, addressed by name:

"pins": {
  "status_led": 48,
  "boot": 0,
  "sys_out": 3
}

Accessed as board.pin("status_led").

docs.title: resources: buses
docs.text:
Each bus type is a dict of named bus instances. The instance name is what firmware code looks up (e.g., board.spi("lcd") returns the lcd entry under spi).

Bus type Fields uart tx, rx, optional rts, cts i2c scl, sda spi sck, mosi, miso, cs, dc, rst qspi sck, data0..3, cs, te i2s mclk, bck, ws, din, dout sdmmc clk, cmd, d0..3 can tx, rx

Example:

"spi": {
  "lcd":      { "sck": 12, "mosi": 11, "miso": 13, "dc": 4, "cs": 10, "rst": 9 },
  "sdcard":   { "sck": 36, "mosi": 35, "miso": 37, "cs":  8 }
}

On a bare dev board, where an i2c, spi, uart or can bus is only where it goes by convention, mark it "default": true. Something the person wires can then take its pins, and the bus is left out while it does. Leave it off a bus with something on it, such as a transceiver or the console UART. See What a Board Tells an Agent.

docs.title: devices
docs.text: Higher-level peripherals. Each entry names a driver and references the bus it's connected to. The most important device entries are shown below.

docs.title: display
docs.text:
The interface field dispatches to the correct init path at boot, and it must be set or the display silently fails to initialize.

"display": {
  "type": "ST7789",            // hardware marking
  "driver": "st7789",          // firmware driver module: st7789, spd2010, co5300, epd
  "bus": "spi.lcd",            // which bus instance from resources.*
  "interface": "spi",          // spi | qspi | epd, REQUIRED, selects init path
  "width": 240,
  "height": 240,
  "offset_x": 0,               // origin offset in the controller's RAM
  "offset_y": 0,
  "color_bits": 16,
  "rst_pin": 9,                // reset GPIO (QSPI/AMOLED drivers)
  "te_pin": 13,                // tearing-effect sync (QSPI only)
  "backlight": {
    "pin": 5,
    "active_high": true,
    "pwm_capable": true
  },
  "description": "1.3\" 240x240 IPS LCD"
}

Supported driver values: st7789 (SPI IPS LCDs), spd2010 (QSPI round LCDs with touch), co5300 (1.75" QSPI AMOLED), epd (e-paper).

Agents read each device's description, so a display's should say how to draw on it. On the QSPI boards, boot starts LVGL on the panel, and their descriptions tell agents to use it.

docs.title: status_led
docs.text:
"status_led": {
  "type": "neopixel",
  "pin": 48,
  "pixel_order": "GRB",
  "description": "Onboard RGB NeoPixel"
}

For a plain GPIO LED, use "type": "gpio" and add "active_high": true.

docs.title: I²C devices (IMU, RTC, codec, PMU…)
docs.text:
All follow the same shape. bus points to a resources.i2c.* entry, i2c_address is required (MicroPython won't probe), and driver names the Python driver module:

"imu": {
  "type": "QMI8658C",
  "driver": "qmi8658",
  "bus": "i2c.i2c0",
  "i2c_address": "0x6B",
  "int1_pin": 21,
  "description": "6-axis accelerometer/gyroscope"
},
"rtc": {
  "type": "PCF85063",
  "driver": "pcf85063",
  "bus": "i2c.i2c0",
  "i2c_address": "0x51",
  "int_pin": 9,
  "description": "Real-time clock"
}

docs.title: sdcard
docs.text:
"sdcard": {
  "mode": "SDMMC",             // SDMMC or SPI
  "bus": "sdmmc.sdcard",       // or "spi.sdcard"
  "bus_width": 4,              // SDMMC only: 1 or 4
  "description": "microSD (SDMMC 4-bit)"
}

docs.title: memory
docs.text:
Purely informational: Studio uses this to pick the right firmware variant:

"memory": {
  "flash_size": "16MB",
  "psram_size": "8MB",
  "psram_mode": "octal"       // quad | octal | none
}

docs.title: Validation tips
docs.text:
• Pin conflicts: the firmware doesn't check for conflicts between buses and devices; a wrong pin is usually a silent failure. Cross-check against the board's schematic.
  • Missing interface: the display init path depends on this field being present; without it the boot splash is silently skipped (see lib/sys/display/display_manager.py).
  • Testing locally: you can drop a manifest straight into /settings/board.json on the device with the Files view and reboot to try it without committing the file. Keep its identity.revision at or above the published one, or Studio replaces it the next time it connects.
  • Boot log: boot.py logs display and peripheral init errors. If something isn't working, connect to the REPL and check for Display init skipped: … or similar messages.

docs.title: Flashing Firmware
docs.text: Put ScriptO Studio's firmware on a board over USB. You do this from Set up a new board on Home, which opens System > Firmware.

docs.title: Supported chips
docs.text:
The Firmware panel flashes boards with an ESP32-S3 or an ESP32-P4. It reads the chip, the flash size and, on the S3, the in-package PSRAM, then picks the build for you:

Chip Builds ESP32-S3 ESP32_S3_8 (quad PSRAM), ESP32_S3_8_OCT (octal PSRAM), ESP32_S3_16, ESP32_S3_32 ESP32-P4 ESP32_P4_16, ESP32_P4_32

The 16 MB and 32 MB S3 builds need octal PSRAM. A quad PSRAM part gets ESP32_S3_8, even on larger flash.

After you pick the build, a Board Configuration menu lists the board manifests for your chip, with the generic board for that chip selected. Choose your board if it's listed. These are the boards offered:

Chip Boards ESP32-S3 Generic ESP32-S3, RetroVMS Mini, Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3, Waveshare ESP32-S3 Touch LCD 1.46, Touch LCD 1.69, LCD 1.47, ESP32-S3-RLCD-4.2, ePaper 3.97, Touch AMOLED 1.64, 1.75 and 1.75C ESP32-P4 Generic ESP32-P4, Scripto P4+C6, Waveshare ESP32-P4-WIFI6, ESP32-P4-WIFI6-POE-ETH

See Board Configurations for what a manifest holds.

docs.title: Flash a board
docs.text:
You need Chrome or Edge, which provide Web Serial.

  1. On Home, click Set up a new board. This opens System > Firmware.
  2. Plug the board in over USB and click Connect Device. Pick the port in the browser's chooser.
  3. Studio shows the chip, MAC address and flash size under Device Information, then offers four options:
    • Flash Device: flash fresh firmware onto a blank ESP32.
    • Forgot Credentials: see the saved hostname and WiFi network. See Provisioning.
    • Change WiFi: update network settings on a board that's already set up. See Network Setup.
    • Re-provision: fresh start with new certificates. See Provisioning.
  4. Click Flash Device. Check the firmware and board shown, then click Flash Firmware and confirm. The flash erases everything on the board.
  5. When Flash Complete appears, click Configure WiFi. Pick your network and enter its password.

Studio then generates a certificate and restarts the board into setup mode. The rest is in Provisioning.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The board doesn't connect

  • Use a USB cable that carries data, not a charge-only cable.
  • Try another USB port.

The board doesn't boot after a flash

  • Check that you picked the right build and board.
  • Flash again. The flash erases the board first.
  • Check that the PSRAM type matches the build.

docs.title: Network Setup
docs.text: Set the WiFi network a board joins, and see its network state.

docs.title: Change WiFi over USB
docs.text:
1. On Home, click Set up a new board. This opens System > Firmware.
  2. Plug the board in over USB and click Connect Device.
  3. Choose Change WiFi.
  4. Studio scans and lists the networks it finds.
  5. Pick your network and enter the password.
  6. The board connects and saves the settings, and Studio returns to the options screen.

Changing WiFi only updates the network settings. Run Re-provision if you also want a new certificate. See Provisioning.

The list shows each network's name (SSID), its signal strength in dBm, and a lock for networks that need a password. About -50 dBm is excellent, -70 is fair and -90 is weak.

docs.title: Networks > WiFi
docs.text:
With a board connected, open Networks > WiFi to see its WiFi state:

  • Wi-Fi Client Interface: active or inactive, with MAC address, SSID, IP address, subnet mask, gateway, DNS server and signal strength.
  • Wi-Fi Access Point Interface: active or inactive, with MAC address, SSID, IP address, subnet mask, gateway, DNS server and connected clients.

Other panels under Networks cover Ethernet, VPN, Bluetooth LE, WWAN, MQTT, Telephony, NTP and CAN. You can switch an interface on or off in System > Settings under Network Interfaces. See Settings.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The network doesn't appear

  • The network must broadcast its name. Hidden networks aren't listed.
  • Move the board closer to the router.
  • Go back and choose Change WiFi again to rescan.

The connection fails

The status log says why, as the board reported it: the network refused it, it can't see the network, it lost the signal, or nothing answered in time.

  • Check the password.
  • Check for MAC filtering on your router.
  • Use a 2.4 GHz network.
  • If the board joins only while your finger is on its antenna, lower its transmit power. Some cheap boards need this. In the terminal, run from lib.sys import settings; settings.set("wifi.txpower", 8.5); settings.save(), then reset the board. It takes 2 to 20 dBm, and None puts back the default of 20.

The wrong network was saved

Run Change WiFi again and pick another network.

docs.title: Provisioning
docs.text: Provisioning gives a board its HTTPS certificate and its password. A new board gets this automatically at the end of setup. You can also run it again on its own.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Generates a self-signed HTTPS certificate for https://<hostname>.local, where the hostname looks like pybot-xxxx.
  • Restarts the board into setup mode, where it serves a password page.
  • Sends you to Studio with the board's address filled in.

docs.title: New board
docs.text:
When you set up a new board, WiFi and the certificate happen back to back after the flash:

  1. Studio saves your WiFi settings and the hostname, then generates and installs the certificate.
  2. The board restarts on your network and serves its setup page.
  3. A dialog, Accept Security Warning, offers to open the board. Click the button to open https://<hostname>.local in a new tab.
  4. Your browser warns about the certificate. This is expected, because the certificate is self-signed. Choose Advanced, then Proceed. You do this once per browser.
  5. The page redirects from /setup and asks for a password. Set one (at least 4 characters).
  6. The board restarts and Studio opens with the connect dialog filled in with wss://<hostname>/mcp. Enter the password to connect.

docs.title: Re-provision
docs.text:
Use Re-provision in System > Firmware to:

  • Renew an expired certificate.
  • Make a certificate for a changed hostname.
  • Start fresh with a new certificate and a new password.

Connect the board over USB, choose Re-provision, and follow the same steps as above from the security warning on. Your WiFi settings are kept.

docs.title: Forgot Credentials
docs.text: Choose Forgot Credentials in System > Firmware with the board connected over USB. It shows the board's hostname and the WiFi network it's set to join. It doesn't show the password. If you've lost the password, run Re-provision to set a new one.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The board doesn't appear after the restart

  • Wait 10 to 15 seconds for it to join WiFi.
  • If .local doesn't resolve, open the board by its IP address from your router's device list.

The certificate warning keeps appearing

  • Make sure you chose Proceed.
  • Run Re-provision to make a fresh certificate.

You can't reach the board after provisioning

  • Check that it's on the same network as your computer.
  • Check that the WiFi settings are right with Forgot Credentials.
