docs.title: Set Up a Board and Connect
docs.text: You need an ESP32 board, a USB cable, and Chrome or Edge, because flashing uses Web Serial. Once a board is set up, it connects over your network from any browser.

docs.title: 1. Open Studio
docs.text: Go to scriptostudio.com/app. You can install it as an app from your browser's menu.

docs.title: 2. Set up a new board
docs.text:
1. Plug the board in with USB.
  2. Click Set up a new board at the bottom of the sidebar. That opens System > Firmware.
  3. Follow the steps to flash the firmware and give the board your WiFi details. Its certificate is generated for you.
  4. Choose the board's password at https://<host>.local/setup. Your browser warns about the board's certificate the first time, because the board signed it itself. That's expected, so proceed to it.
  5. The board sends you back to Studio with its address filled in.

See Flashing Firmware and Provisioning for the details.

docs.title: 3. Connect
docs.text:
Click Connect a board, or Connect beside a board you've used before.

  • Device URL is the board's address, such as wss://pybot-6014.local/mcp.
  • Password is the one you chose during setup.

The board then appears in the sidebar with what it has, such as CAN, Clock or Motion, and the ScriptOs on it.

docs.title: 4. Add an API key
docs.text:
Studio's agent runs in your browser and uses models through OpenRouter, on your own account.

  1. Click Add an API key under the message box, and paste your key.
  2. Click the model's name beside it to choose another model. Tick Free only to see the free ones.

The key stays in this browser, in a separate frame that Studio's pages and Apps can't read.

If you'd rather use Claude Code or another agent, see Other Agents. You don't need a key for that.

docs.title: 5. Ask for something
docs.text:
Type what the board should do, or pick a suggestion. Suggestions come from what the board says it has.

Next: Your First ScriptO.

docs.title: Your First ScriptO
docs.text: This walks through one request on a board with an accelerometer and a buzzer. On another board, ask for something it has hardware for.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
On Home, type:

Beep when the board is tilted

docs.title: Watch
docs.text:
The chat shows each call the agent makes, and the terminal shows the code it runs and what that printed.

  1. It tries the hardware. It calls exec to read the accelerometer and see what it reads at rest.
  2. It leaves a ScriptO. It calls scripto_create with an id and the code. The code is checked before anything is written, so a mistake can't replace what's working.
  3. Studio checks on it. Two seconds after a ScriptO starts, Studio tells the agent what became of it. If it crashed, the agent sees the error and can fix it.
  4. It reports. It says what it did and what it couldn't check. An agent can't hear a buzzer, so it asks you to try it.

The ScriptO's row appears in the sidebar, marked Running.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Tilt the board. It should beep once per tilt.

If it doesn't do what you wanted, say so in the same chat. The agent can read the sensor again, change the code and restart it.

docs.title: Keep it
docs.text:
The ScriptO keeps running after you close Studio. To have it start every time the board powers up, tick At startup on its row, or ask the agent.

From the row you can also:

  • Stop or Start it.
  • Read its code with Code, which opens it in the Editor.
  • Remove it, which deletes its code and leaves its data.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text: The code is at /lib/ext/<folder>/main.py, and /lib/ext/registry.json records what's installed. See ScriptOs.

docs.title: The menu, on the left
docs.text:
• Home is the chat with Studio's agent.
  • Editor edits and runs code, with a debugger. See Editor.
  • Files moves files between the board and your browser's storage. See Files.
  • Networks configures WiFi, Ethernet, VPN, Bluetooth LE, WWAN, MQTT, Telephony, NTP and CAN.
  • Peripherals configures GPS, Modem and SD Card.
  • System has About, Settings, Agent and Firmware.
  • Apps lists what's installed, and + adds more.

The language selector is at the bottom.

docs.title: The main pane, in the centre
docs.text: Whatever you pick from the menu appears here. The chat waits on Home while you're elsewhere, and a banner on other views tells you when it needs an answer.

docs.title: The sidebar, on the right
docs.text:
It stays in every view:

  • The board and what it has, or a list of boards you've used when none is connected.
  • ScriptOs, each with Start or Stop, At startup, Code and Remove.
  • The terminal, the board's one REPL, once a board is connected. See Terminal.

Drag the divider on its left to make it wider, for long terminal output. Studio remembers the width.

docs.title: Stopping things
docs.text:
• Stop in the chat ends Studio's agent and its call, and leaves everything else running.
  • Stop above the editor, and under Other agents on Home, breaks whatever is running, whichever client started it, and stops ScriptOs and Apps as well.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
What boards does it run on? ESP32 boards running Studio's firmware. System > Firmware lists what can be flashed, and Board Configurations describes the board manifests.

Which browser do I need? Any modern browser can connect to a board. Flashing firmware over USB needs Chrome or Edge, because it uses Web Serial.

Does a board need Studio to keep running? No. A ScriptO keeps running with nobody connected, and one set to start at boot runs even with no network.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Do I need an API key? For Studio's agent, yes, an OpenRouter key. For an outside agent like Claude Code, no: it uses its own account.

What does it cost? Studio's agent is billed to your OpenRouter account. OpenRouter has free models with daily limits. Every round of tool calls sends the chat so far, so long chats cost more, and Studio summarises them to keep that down.

Which model should I use? Any model that supports tools can work. They vary in how well they use tools, so try another if one struggles.

Can an agent damage my board? exec runs any Python, so it could erase files or drive a pin. Studio's agent asks before what's plainly hard to undo, and you can Stop it at any moment, but that guards against accidents and isn't a sandbox. Follow what's wired to the board, and don't leave an agent alone with anything that could cause harm.

Where does my chat go? To the model you chose, through OpenRouter. It's stored in this browser, one chat per board, until you click New chat. It includes whatever the board printed.

Can I use my key on another computer? The key stays in the browser you entered it in, so add it again there.

docs.title: ScriptOs and Apps
docs.text:
What's the difference? A ScriptO is MicroPython on the board. An App has a browser side as well. See Apps.

Where is a ScriptO's code? In /lib/ext/<folder>/main.py. Code on its row opens it.

I changed the code and nothing happened. A running ScriptO keeps running the old code. Stop it and Start it.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text: See Connection Issues.

docs.title: MCP Tools
docs.text: A board is an MCP server at /mcp. It speaks the 2026-07-28 revision and the older initialize handshake, so a stock MCP client needs nothing specific to Studio.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Group Tools Notes Run code exec Runs in __main__. Returns output and any traceback Files fs_list, fs_stat, fs_read_text, fs_write_text, fs_rm, fs_mkdir, fs_hash Writes go to a temporary file and are renamed, so a half-written file never replaces the real one Board device_info, logs_read, reset reset takes soft or hard. After changing files in lib/sys, use hard, since soft keeps loaded modules What's wired wired_add, wired_remove See below ScriptOs scriptos_list, scripto_create, scripto_installed, scripto_run_at_boot, scripto_start, scripto_stop, scripto_remove See below Jobs job_start, job_status, job_cancel For a ScriptO's long tools Stopping interrupt, stop_user_tasks Separate, so an agent can end its own call without stopping anyone's ScriptOs Updates update_check, update_start, update_status, update_cancel The platform, from ScriptoHub. See below Wi-Fi, a person's only wifi_status, wifi_scan, wifi_join, wifi_forget Put a board on another network, over any carrier. See below Built in, where the board has the hardware can_capture Finds a CAN signal from what changes From what's installed <scripto>_<tool> Change as ScriptOs and Apps are installed

device_info returns everything about the board's hardware, and the same facts arrive in the server's instructions. See What a Board Tells an Agent.

docs.title: scripto_create
docs.text:
Argument Meaning id Required. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens code Required. Has to define async def run() name, version For showing to people run_at_boot Start it at every boot start Start it now. On unless set to false tools Tool files to write, by name

It compiles the code before it writes anything, then writes atomically, registers the ScriptO and starts it. It answers before the code has run, so look at scriptos_list and logs_read to see what became of it.

docs.title: wired_add
docs.text:
Argument Meaning name Required. Lowercase letters, digits and underscores. The same name replaces what's there entry Required. Like a manifest device: type, description, and its GPIOs as pin or <role>_pin, or bus and i2c_address to share a bus kind device, the default, or i2c, spi, uart or can for a bus on pins of its own, which devices then name

It writes /settings/wired.json and reloads the board module, so board.pin() and board.device() find the entry at once, and the next client to connect sees it. It refuses a pin the board or something already wired uses, and on an ESP32-S3 GPIO 26 to 37, which flash and PSRAM hold. A description is at most 300 characters, and at most 16 things can be wired. Its notes say which default bus, if any, it took a pin from. See What a Board Tells an Agent.

wired_remove takes out one entry by name, but not a bus a wired device still names. Helper files stay.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
These update the platform, the firmware and botIQ, from a ScriptoHub platform release. Studio and CaffiPod both use them. The code is lib/sys/update.py.

Tool What it does update_check What a release would change, writing nothing: newer or not, whether the firmware changes or needs USB, and what apps say against updating now. A job, since it fetches and hashes update_start Starts the update in the background, the newest of the board's major or version. Refused while an app says now isn't safe update_status State, bytes done, what it waits on, how the last update ended, the installed release update_cancel Stops a download. Starting the same release again resumes it

The board takes a release only when a key built into its firmware signed the release's file list, and checks every file and the image against their sha256 as they lie in flash. The image goes into the spare app slot, and changed files go into place with the old ones kept in /update/backup. The board then restarts on trial: once the MCP core answers and the apps that ran at boot run again, the release is kept. Otherwise the next restart goes back to the old slot, and the firmware puts the old files back before botIQ loads: that step is frozen into pyDirect's firmware, so no file on the board can break it. A board with one app slot (8 MB) takes framework files only, and its firmware needs USB.

An app says when an update may write flash or restart:

from lib.sys import update
update.ask_before("myapp", lambda: None if idle() else "a run is going")

The function returns None when now is safe, or why not. It's asked before the update starts, before every flash write and before the restart, and the update waits while any app says no.

A release may write only botIQ's files: main.py and lib/, except lib/ext/ (apps) and lib/wired/. Settings, certificates and data are never touched.

docs.title: Wi-Fi
docs.text:
These put a board on a new network: after a move, or a new router. CaffiPod uses them over Bluetooth, so a board with no Wi-Fi at all can be given some, and Studio can use them over any carrier. The code is lib/sys/network/wifi.py.

Tool What it does wifi_status connected; while connected, the network's name ssid, ip and rssi (dBm); saved, the network it joins at boot; joining, a join under way; last_join, how the last one ended: {ssid, ok, ip} or {ssid, ok, reason} wifi_scan networks the board can see: one row per name at its strongest, strongest first, each {ssid, rssi, secured, channel}. A few seconds wifi_join ssid and password (empty or left out for an open network). Answers {ssid, ip} once the board has an address there, and only then saves the network. Within about 30 s wifi_forget Forgets the saved network, password and all, and leaves it: {forgot}, the name or null
  • A person's only. An agent's call is refused, and an agent doesn't see these tools listed. They're marked for an app's screens, not a model.
  • A refusal is the tool failing with the bare reason, for a client to match: wrong password, no such network (not in sight and nothing answered), timeout, refused (the driver gave up for another reason), busy (a join is under way), not saved, stopped, or bad request: …. A failed join leaves the saved network as it was, and the board goes back to it.
  • The password goes to the Wi-Fi driver and to settings only: never into a result, a log line, a notification or the terminal.
  • They answer when they're done. The call runs as a task, and the pump moves on meanwhile, so a board's apps keep running. That needs a held connection: WebSocket, WebRTC or Bluetooth. Over plain HTTP they refuse, except wifi_status.
  • While a call uses the radio, the Wi-Fi task waits, giving up any attempt it was making. A scan stops an attempt that's under way, since the driver can't scan while it connects.
  • Over Wi-Fi itself, a join drops the connection as the board leaves its network. The join carries on; read its outcome with wifi_status once back.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
WebSocket, wss or ws Plain HTTP POST Used by Studio, Studio's agent, ss-relay Claude Code, other HTTP clients Streams and push notifications Yes No A ScriptO's long tool Stays open, with progress Returns a job id to poll The name a person sees The client's own agent Breaking its own blocked exec Yes No. The 4 second timer ends it Encryption With wss None

A board holds three WebSockets. A fourth client is refused with a close frame saying why, and nobody is pushed off.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
There are two roles, and both come from the board's password. Each token is the first 32 hex characters of sha256("ss-<role>:<password>"), with the role human or agent.

An HTTP client sends Authorization: Bearer <token>. A WebSocket client offers the subprotocols mcp and ss.<token>.

Agent token Human token exec limit 4 s Up to 60 s Can break Its own call Anyone's call Can arm CAN transmit No Yes Receives the activity feed No Yes Its calls are reported to people Yes No

This is authentication plus a person watching. It isn't a sandbox, because exec runs any Python.

docs.title: CAN transmit
docs.text: can.agent_tx_needs_arm is off by default. With it set, an agent's transmits are refused until a person arms them.

docs.title: ScriptOs
docs.text: A ScriptO is MicroPython left on the board to stay. It runs with nobody connected and can start at boot, and it's what an agent leaves behind.

docs.title: What one is made of
docs.text:
Part Where it lives What it does Its own work /lib/ext/<folder>/main.py, with async def run() Runs as a user task, with nobody connected Tools for agents /lib/ext/<folder>/tools/<name>.py Appear to any agent as <scripto>_<name> Startup record run_at_boot in /lib/ext/registry.json Starts it at every boot

A ScriptO needs at least one of main.py or a tool. See Writing ScriptOs.

docs.title: In the sidebar
docs.text:
Each ScriptO has a row with its state: Running, Stopped, Not started or Crashed, and why it stopped.

  • Start and Stop
  • At startup to run it at boot
  • Code to open it in the Editor
  • Remove to delete its code. Its data stays.
  • Ask agent, when it has crashed, to attach the error to your next message

docs.title: At boot
docs.text: The board starts its boot ScriptOs before it brings up the network or the servers, so one still runs where there's no WiFi.

docs.title: What bad code can do
docs.text: Failure What happens A Python exception Shown on its row and in scriptos_list, then retried It holds the event loop The watchdog names it in the log, then breaks it about 5 seconds later A crash in C Crash resets are counted. After 3 in a row the board starts without its boot ScriptOs, and Studio says why

docs.title: ScriptOs and Apps
docs.text: An App is a ScriptO with a browser side as well, written in JavaScript, for tools that need a screen. Agents make ScriptOs and don't write Apps.

docs.title: UI plugin: Hello World
docs.text: A ScriptO can serve its own web page from the board and ask Studio to show it in a window. This example registers an HTTP route and opens a page in a modal over Studio.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The ScriptO registers an HTTP route (/hello_ui) on the board's web server.
  2. It sends Studio a display_ui event with events.notify.
  3. Studio opens a modal that loads the board's URL in an iframe.
  4. The page is served by the board.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Ask the agent on Home to make it, or put the code below in a file in the Editor and click Run. The page opens in a modal over Studio. To keep it on the board as a ScriptO, ask the agent to leave it there with scripto_create.

The code is the template below. Change title and the HTML to make your own.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
import json

import httpserver

from lib.sys import events
from lib.sys.utils import getDeviceURL


def my_ui_handler(uri, post_data=None, remote_addr=None):
    html = """<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>My Custom UI</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: sans-serif; padding: 24px; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello from the board</h1>
    <script>
        // Your JavaScript here
    </script>
</body>
</html>"""
    httpserver.send(html)


httpserver.on('/my_ui', my_ui_handler, 'GET')

events.notify({
    "display_ui": {
        "url": getDeviceURL('/my_ui'),
        "title": "My Custom UI"
    }
})

docs.title: Key functions
docs.text: Function Module Purpose httpserver.on(path, handler, method) httpserver Register an HTTP route httpserver.send(content) httpserver Send the HTTP response getDeviceURL(path) lib.sys.utils The board's URL with the right protocol and its .local hostname events.notify(event) lib.sys.events Send an event to every connected client

docs.title: Trust the board's certificate
docs.text:
The board's HTTPS certificate is its own, so Chrome may show "Not Secure" in the address bar when the page loads. This is cosmetic. To clear it on a Mac:

  1. In Files, open /certs/ and download servercert.pem.
  2. Double-click the file to add it to Keychain Access.
  3. Find the certificate there, double-click it and expand Trust.
  4. Set When using this certificate to Always Trust, and close the dialog.
  5. Restart Chrome.

Each board has its own certificate, so repeat this for each one you want to trust.

docs.title: Sharing the interpreter
docs.text: Everything on the board runs in one MicroPython interpreter, so your ScriptO shares it with the system. This page covers what that means for the code you write.

docs.title: One interpreter, cooperative multitasking
docs.text:
The board runs asyncio. Only one task executes at a time, and a task gives up the interpreter when it awaits.

asyncio event loop
    ├── queue_pump()      serves MCP and HTTP every 10 ms
    ├── network tasks     WiFi, Ethernet and the like
    └── your ScriptO      its run() in /lib/ext/<folder>/main.py
Component Runs as Yields by Queue pump System task, a 10 ms loop await asyncio.sleep_ms(10) Your ScriptO User task Your awaits exec calls from an agent or Studio Synchronous, on the interpreter thread Running to completion

[!IMPORTANT] A loop with no await freezes everything, including the queue pump. Agents and Studio can't reach the board until it yields. If something holds the event loop too long, the watchdog breaks it with a KeyboardInterrupt and the ScriptO stops with the reason "it held the event loop too long".

An exec call is stopped after 4 seconds by default, because a longer block would make the watchdog stop user tasks. Put long work in a ScriptO and await in it.

docs.title: The queue pump
docs.text:
queue_pump() in lib/sys/app.py is a system task:

async def queue_pump():
    while True:
        if mcp.started():
            httpserver.process_queue()   # MCP over WebSocket and HTTP, and any routes you add
            mcp.after_pump()
        await asyncio.sleep_ms(10)
        bg_tasks.feed("queue_pump")

Every tool call, from an agent or from Studio, is handled here. The task feeds a watchdog on each pass, which is how a ScriptO that holds the loop gets caught.

docs.title: Writing a ScriptO that yields
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def run():
    while True:
        do_work()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

Don't use time.sleep() in a loop. It blocks the interpreter and doesn't yield.

docs.title: System and user tasks
docs.text:
lib/sys/bg_tasks.py keeps the board's tasks by name. A ScriptO's run() runs as a user task named app_<id>.

Type Stopped by System (is_system=True) Only bg_tasks.stop_all() User (is_system=False) The Stop button, Ctrl+C, a watchdog break, a reset 
from lib.sys import bg_tasks

bg_tasks.start("my_animation", animate_leds)                  # user task
bg_tasks.start("monitor", monitor, is_system=True)            # survives Stop

Useful calls: stop(name), stop_user_tasks(), is_running(name), list_tasks(), and feed(name) to feed a task's watchdog from inside its loop. Stop, above the editor, calls stop_user_tasks().

docs.title: Task lifecycle
docs.text:
A user task that raises is marked crashed. It restarts after one second, and the ScriptO's row in the sidebar shows it as crashed with the restart count and last error. A task that returns ends as stopped. A task that's stopped by Stop or a break records why it stopped.

If the board crashes three times in a row at boot, it starts without its run-at-boot ScriptOs and says so in each one's status. A reset tries again.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
_thread works, but use it rarely. The status LED animation runs in a thread, and that pattern is safe because it's created once at boot, reads a singleton, does short bounded work and sleeps each pass.

  • Don't use await, asyncio or the network from a thread.
  • Don't share mutable data between threads without a flag or lock.
  • A thread can't be joined or killed, and an uncaught exception ends it silently.
  • Create threads once and reuse them. Creating and destroying them fragments the heap.

For nearly everything else, use an asyncio task.

docs.title: Bus Sharing (I2C / SPI)
docs.text: When multiple Apps or ScriptOs talk to devices on the same I2C or SPI bus, they must share a single machine.I2C or machine.SPI instance. If two of them each create their own instance for the same hardware peripheral, the second one silently reconfigures the bus, potentially breaking the first.

docs.title: Why No Locking Is Needed
docs.text:
In CircuitPython, the busio.I2C class has try_lock() / unlock() methods because its USB stack can preempt a transaction mid-byte. MicroPython doesn't have this problem, all I2C/SPI calls are synchronous C functions that run to completion. Since the VM is single-threaded and cooperative, no other coroutine can interleave on the bus between await points.

The real risk is configuration conflicts, not data races. The bus module solves this with a singleton cache.

docs.title: The bus Module
docs.text:
from lib.sys import bus

# Board-manifest-aware (recommended: uses board.json pin definitions)
i2c = bus.get_i2c("sensors")

# Explicit pins
i2c = bus.get_i2c(0, scl=9, sda=8, freq=400000)

# SPI works the same way
spi = bus.get_spi("display")
spi = bus.get_spi(1, sck=12, mosi=11, miso=13, baudrate=10000000)

Calling bus.get_i2c("sensors") twice returns the same object, no reconfiguration, no conflicts.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Approach What Happens machine.I2C(0, scl=Pin(9), sda=Pin(8)) × 2 Second call may reconfigure the peripheral bus.get_i2c(0, scl=9, sda=8) × 2 Returns the same cached instance bus.get_i2c("sensors") × 2 Same, using board manifest pins

docs.title: Utility Functions
docs.text:
bus.info()                  # Print all cached buses
bus.release_i2c("sensors")  # Remove from cache (doesn't deinit hardware)

Tip

Always prefer the named form (bus.get_i2c("sensors")) over explicit pins. This keeps your ScriptOs portable across different boards.

docs.title: Writing ScriptOs
docs.text: An agent will usually write these for you. This is what it's writing, for when you want to read or change one yourself.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
A ScriptO's main.py defines async def run():

import asyncio
from lib.sys import imu, buzzer

async def run():
    while True:
        x, y, z = imu.read()
        if abs(x) > 500:
            buzzer.beep(200)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

All Python on the board runs on one thread, shared with the server that Studio and agents talk to. So:

  • Await often. Code that doesn't await holds up every client and ScriptO, and the watchdog breaks it after a few seconds.
  • Use await asyncio.sleep(), never time.sleep().
  • Get pins from the board. Use lib.sys.board, as in board.pin("status_led") and board.i2c("i2c0").scl, or the helper a device's description names.

This is MicroPython, so there's no os.path. See the MicroPython Reference.

docs.title: Making one yourself
docs.text:
In the terminal:

from lib.sys import apps
apps.create("my-scripto", open("/my_code.py").read(), name="My ScriptO")
apps.start("my-scripto")

An id is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. The code is compiled before anything is written, so a mistake can't replace what's working.

docs.title: Changing one
docs.text:
Click Code on its row, edit it and save. A running ScriptO keeps running the old code until you Stop and Start it.

Leave /main.py alone

The board's own /main.py and /boot.py start its server. If you break them, you can't connect. A ScriptO's code goes in its own folder under /lib/ext/.

docs.title: Giving agents a tool
docs.text:
A file at /lib/ext/<folder>/tools/<name>.py appears to any agent as <scripto>_<name>. Its config block becomes the tool's schema:

# === START_CONFIG_PARAMETERS ===
dict(
    info = dict(
        name = "Read parameter",
        description = "What an agent reads to decide to use this.",
        effects = dict(readOnly=True, destructive=False, openWorld=False),
    ),
    args = dict(
        name = dict(label="Parameter name", type=str),
        pin = dict(label="Pin", type=list, optional=True),
        mode = dict(label="Mode", type=dict, items=dict(a="First", b="Second"), value="a"),
    ),
)
# === END_CONFIG_PARAMETERS ===

async def run(args, job):
    job.progress(1, 2, "halfway")
    return {"value": 1}

type=list means a GPIO, with its choices taken from the board's manifest. Files starting with _ aren't tools.

A tool runs as a task, so it can take as long as it needs. A client on a WebSocket stays on the call and gets progress. A client on plain HTTP gets a job id to poll with job_status.

docs.title: Reading CAN
docs.text:
lib.sys.can_tap lets a ScriptO watch the bus without getting in the way of anything else:

from lib.sys import can_tap

watcher = can_tap.watch([0x470])
for can_id, data in watcher.read():
    ...

read() never waits. watch([]) gets every identifier, and watcher.lost() says how many frames it was too slow for.

docs.title: Can't connect to the board
docs.text:
Check these in order:

  1. The address. It should look like wss://pybot-6014.local/mcp. Studio adds /mcp for you.
  2. The network. The board and your computer need to be on the same network. If the .local name doesn't resolve, try the board's IP address.
  3. The certificate. The board signs its own certificate, so your browser refuses it until you've accepted it once. Open https://<host>/ in a tab, proceed past the warning, then try again. The connection dialog offers a link to this.
  4. The password. It's the one you chose at setup.

docs.title: "This board doesn't accept connections from..."
docs.text: The board only accepts WebSockets from Studio's own addresses. If you're running Studio from somewhere else, add that address to the board's server.allowed_origins setting.

docs.title: The board refuses another client
docs.text: A board holds three WebSockets. A fourth client is refused with a message saying why, and nobody is pushed off. Studio holds one, and a second once its agent has run, until you press Stop or start a New chat. Close another client on your computer, or use plain HTTP for it, which holds none between calls.

docs.title: Forgot the password
docs.text: Connect the board by USB and open System > Firmware. Re-provision gives the board new certificates and a new password, and keeps its WiFi settings. Change WiFi changes only the network. See Provisioning.

docs.title: Studio's agent
docs.text:
It says it needs a key. Click Add an API key under the message box.

"Your OpenRouter account is out of credits." Add credit at OpenRouter, or pick a free model.

A free model stops with a rate limit. Free models have daily limits. Wait, or choose another model.

"Connect a board, and an agent can get to work on it." Studio needs a board connected before the agent can start. A saved chat still shows while you're disconnected.

docs.title: An outside agent
docs.text:
It can't reach the board. Check that the address and token match System > Agent. They change if you change the board's password.

A tool is missing or "Unknown tool". A session can keep the tool list it started with. Start a new session.

It connected to the wrong board. Each claude mcp add line names one board. See what's configured with claude mcp list.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: The debugger runs the file you're editing on the board and stops it at breakpoints. At each stop you see the watch expressions and the variables, and you choose how to go on.

docs.title: Start a session
docs.text:
1. Connect a board and open a Python file in the Editor.
  2. Optionally, set breakpoints in the gutter (below).
  3. Click Debug in the toolbar. The Setup Debugger sidebar opens. It's available only in the Editor view, with a board connected and a file open.
  4. Add watch expressions if you want them.
  5. Click Start Debugging, or click Run in the toolbar.

Studio prepares the file in the browser, interrupts whatever is running, and runs the prepared file in the terminal. While a session is open the editor is read-only, and New and Save are disabled.

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text:
Click the gutter beside a line number to set a breakpoint. A marker appears in the gutter, and the line gets a # ● comment at its end. Click the marker to open the breakpoint dialog:

Field Meaning Enabled switch Turns the breakpoint on or off without removing it. Condition An expression, for example x == 0. The breakpoint stops only when it's true. Hit count Stops by count: <1, <=2, =3, >4, >=5 or %6. Trash button Deletes the breakpoint.

Click Save to keep your changes.

docs.title: Watch expressions
docs.text: Watch Expressions takes one expression per line, for example x * 2. Studio evaluates them each time the program stops.

docs.title: While the program is stopped
docs.text:
The toolbar shows these buttons during a session:

Button Action Stop End the session and interrupt the board. Continue Run until the next breakpoint. F5. Step Step over the current line. F10. Step In Step into a call. F11. Step Out Run until the current function returns. F12.

The sidebar, titled Debug Session, shows Live Variables: your watch expressions and the local variables at the stop. The terminal prints the stop as well, with the file and line, the watches, the locals, the memory in use and the elapsed time.

docs.title: How it connects
docs.text: The prepared file runs on the terminal stream. The board reports each stop on that stream, and Studio sends Continue and the step commands back through the exec tool. See MCP tools.

docs.title: Editor Features
docs.text:
The Editor edits files on the board or in your browser storage. Open it with Editor in the menu.

The editor is CodeMirror 6. It has Python and JSON highlighting, line numbers, folding, bracket matching, search and undo history.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text: Button Action Shortcut New Create a file. Ctrl+N / Cmd+N Save Save the current file. Ctrl+S / Cmd+S Reset Reset the board. Stop Interrupt what's running and stop background tasks. Run Run the current file on the board. Ctrl+R / Cmd+R Debug Start a debug session. See Debugging.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Each open file has a tab. A CPU icon means the file is on the board, and a desktop icon means it's in browser storage. A * marks unsaved changes.

  • Click a tab to switch to it.
  • Click the name on the active tab to rename the file.
  • Click the x to close it.

docs.title: Run
docs.text: Run sends the editor's current text to the board, saved or not. Output appears in the terminal in the sidebar.

docs.title: JSON mode
docs.text: Files that end in .json get JSON highlighting. When you open one that holds a JSON object or array, Studio reformats it with two-space indentation.

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text: Click the gutter beside a line number to set a breakpoint. See Debugging.

docs.title: Other shortcuts
docs.text:
Shortcut Action Ctrl+L / Cmd+L Clear the terminal.

These act in the Editor, apart from clearing the terminal, so Cmd+R reloads the page anywhere else. Browsers keep Cmd+N for themselves in a tab, so that one needs Studio installed as an app.

docs.title: File Manager
docs.text:
The File Manager shows the board's files next to files kept in your browser, and moves files between them.

Open it with Files in the menu.

docs.title: The two panes
docs.text:
Pane Shows Left The board's filesystem. It reads Connect to board until a board is connected. Right Browser storage: files Studio keeps in your browser, on your computer.

Each pane has a header with its path and three buttons: new folder, new file, and upload (left pane) or import (right pane). Files show their size. Folders are listed first.

Between the panes is a column of buttons that act on what you've selected:

Button Action Edit (pencil) Open the selected files in the editor. Left arrow Copy the selection from browser storage to the board. Right arrow Copy the selection from the board to browser storage. Down arrow Export the selected files to your computer, as browser downloads. Trash Delete the selection.

docs.title: Select, open and navigate
docs.text:
• Click an item to select it. Click it again to clear it.
  • Double-click a file to open it in the editor.
  • Double-click a folder to go into it. Click .. at the top of the list to go up.

docs.title: Create, rename and delete
docs.text:
• New file and New folder add an empty entry to the list with a name field. Type a name and press Enter. Press Escape to cancel.
  • Rename: click the text-cursor icon at the end of a row, edit the name, and press Enter.
  • Delete: select items, click the trash button and confirm. The confirmation lists what will go.

[!WARNING] Deleting boot.py or breaking main.py can keep the board from starting.

docs.title: Move files
docs.text:
• Copy to the board or to browser storage with the arrow buttons. If a file of the same name is already at the destination, Studio lists the files it would overwrite and asks first.
  • Upload (left pane header) sends files from your computer straight to the board.
  • Import (right pane header) brings files from your computer into browser storage.
  • Export (down arrow) saves the selected files from either pane to your computer.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: System > Settings holds the options for how Studio looks and which network interfaces the board starts. Changes to appearance apply at once.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
• Theme: Light, Dark or Device, which follows your system.
  • Color Scheme: the accent color. Choose Teal, Blue, Purple, Green, Red or Orange.
  • Editor Theme: the code editor's colors. Auto matches the app theme. The others are Cobalt, Xcode and Cool Glow.
  • Temperature Unit: show temperatures in Celsius or Fahrenheit.

docs.title: Network Interfaces
docs.text: With a board connected, Network Interfaces lists WiFi, and Ethernet and WWAN (4G) on boards that have them. Switch an interface off and a disabled one won't start at boot. At least one must stay on. Click Save Network Settings to send the choice to the board.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text: Studio has one terminal, a MicroPython REPL on the connected board. It sits in the sidebar on the right, under the board and its ScriptOs, and stays there in every view: Home, Files, the Editor, panels and Apps.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
Click in the terminal and type, as you would at a MicroPython prompt. Output from Run in the editor appears here, along with error messages and tracebacks.

The buttons above the terminal:

Button Action Copy Copy the selected text. Paste Paste into the prompt. Clean Clear the terminal. Shortcut: Ctrl+L or Cmd+L. Toggle Logs Show or hide the Logs list beside the terminal.

The arrow at the end of the bar closes the terminal and opens it again.

docs.title: Resize it
docs.text: Drag the handle in the terminal's bar up or down to change its height. Drag the vertical divider between the main area and the sidebar to change the sidebar's width. Studio remembers the width.

docs.title: What an agent does
docs.text:
When an agent runs code on the board, the code and its output appear in this terminal. Each line is tagged with the name the agent's client gives itself, in square brackets, for example [Claude Code]. Calls an agent makes also show in the Logs list. If the terminal is closed when an agent starts working, it opens.

Stop is above the editor. It interrupts what's running in the terminal and stops background tasks, whoever started them.
